# Treating Heavy Motor Oil Contamination in Laundry

Mixing shop clothes soaked in motor oil with your regular laundry is a technical failure of the wash cycle. The hydrophobic nature of petroleum-based lubricants prevents them from interacting with standard surfactants designed for water-soluble soils like sweat and food particles. When these fabrics hit a mixed load, the oil spreads across the drum, coating lighter garments and creating a massive cleanup effort that requires running the machine again or performing an emergency wash cycle on clean clothes.

To isolate contaminated items effectively, you must treat them as hazardous waste until the hydrocarbons are broken down chemically. The most effective strategy is a dedicated pretreatment phase before any agitation occurs. Start by removing all dry dirt and loose debris from pockets and zippers; this physical removal prevents re-depositing grit into the fibers during the soak. Once the items are prepped, move them to a separate basin or large container filled with warm water—ideally between 140°F (60°C) and 160°F (70°C). Hotter temperatures are often necessary because they reduce the viscosity of the oil, allowing it to penetrate the fabric more easily for extraction.

The chemical agent for this process is critical. Standard laundry detergent alone will not suffice; you need a degreaser or a solvent-based cleaner specifically formulated to break down hydrocarbons. If using a biological enzyme cleaner, ensure it contains lipases and proteases capable of emulsifying the oil. Alternatively, a small amount of dish soap containing surfactants can work in a pinch, but dedicated industrial degreasers are far more effective for heavy saturation.

Apply the cleaning agent directly to the fabric before immersing them. Scrubbing the stained areas gently helps lift the bulk of the oil from the weave without pushing it deeper into the fibers. After application, let the items soak for at least 30 minutes. For heavily saturated workwear, an overnight soak is preferable. During this time, the surfactants lower the surface tension of the water, allowing the solution to penetrate the fabric matrix and surround oil droplets, lifting them away from the textile.

Once the soaking period concludes, inspect the garments. If significant oil remains, repeat the application and soak cycle. Only after the visible sheen is gone should you proceed to a full wash cycle. At this stage, you can safely add these items to your main load with regular laundry, provided the water temperature matches or exceeds that of the pretreatment step. Mixing them now poses little risk because the bulk of the contaminant has already been removed.

However, there are constraints to consider regarding fabric types and disposal. Cotton and denim generally tolerate high-temperature washes well, but synthetic blends or wool may shrink or degrade under extreme heat. Check garment labels for maximum temperature limits; if 160°F is too aggressive, lower the temperature but extend the soaking time accordingly. Additionally, never pour the oily rinse water down a standard drain without checking local regulations, as hydrocarbons can contaminate municipal wastewater systems. Some regions require specific disposal methods for oil-laden washwater to prevent environmental harm.

If you operate a business or manage a team where this is a frequent occurrence, investing in a dedicated machine or a specific detergent line becomes necessary rather than relying on household solutions. For individual users, the key is strict segregation and adequate dwell time during pretreatment. Following this protocol ensures your regular clothes remain clean while effectively removing stubborn shop grime without damaging either set of fabrics.
